arXiv:0904.2813v1 [math.AP] 18 Apr 2009

Diophantine Conditions in Well-Posedness Theory of Coupled KdV-Type Systems: Local Theory

Tadahiro Oh Address: Tadahiro Oh
Department of Mathematics
University of Toronto
40 St. George St, Rm 6290, Toronto, ON M5S 2E4, Canada Email address: oh@math.toronto.edu
Abstract.

We consider the local well-posedness problem of a one-parameter family of coupled KdV-type systems both in the periodic and non-periodic setting. In particular, we show that certain resonances occur, closely depending on the value of a coupling parameter α\alpha when α≠1\alpha\neq 1. In the periodic setting, we use the Diophantine conditions to characterize the resonances, and establish sharp local well-posedness of the system in Hs​(𝕋λ),s≥s∗H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}),s\geq s^{\ast}, where s∗=s∗​(α)∈(12,1]s^{\ast}=s^{\ast}(\alpha)\in(\frac{1}{2},1] is determined by the Diophantine characterization of certain constants derived from the coupling parameter α\alpha. We also present a sharp local (and global) result in L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}). In the appendix, we briefly discuss the local well-posedness result in H−12​(𝕋λ)H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for α=1\alpha=1 without the mean 0 assumption, by introducing the vector-valued Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces.

Key words and phrases: 
KdV; well-posedness; ill-posedness; bilinear estimate; Diophantine condition

35Q53

1. Introduction

In this paper, we consider the local well-posedness (LWP) in both periodic and non-periodic settings of coupled KdV systems of the form:

(1) {ut+a11​ux​x​x+a12​vx​x​x+b1​u​ux+b2​u​vx+b3​ux​v+b4​v​vx=0vt+a21​ux​x​x+a22​vx​x​x+b5​u​ux+b6​u​vx+b7​ux​v+b8​v​vx=0(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\begin{cases}u_{t}+a_{11}u_{xxx}+a_{12}v_{xxx}+b_{1}uu_{x}+b_{2}uv_{x}+b_{3}u_{x}v+b_{4}vv_{x}=0\\ v_{t}+a_{21}u_{xxx}+a_{22}v_{xxx}+b_{5}uu_{x}+b_{6}uv_{x}+b_{7}u_{x}v+b_{8}vv_{x}=0\\ (u,v)\big|_{t=0}=(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{cases}

where A=(a11a12a21a22)A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) is self-adjoint and non-singular, and uu and vv are real-valued functions. There are several systems of this type: the Gear-Grimshaw system [13], the Hirota-Satsuma system [14], the Majda-Biello system [20], etc. Now, write AA as A=M−1​D​MA=M^{-1}DM where D=(d100d2)D=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}d_{1}&0\\ 0&d_{2}\end{smallmatrix}\big) with dj∈ℝ∖{0}d_{j}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and MM is orthogonal. Then, by letting M⁡(uv)​(x,d1−1​t)↦(uv)​(x,t)M\big(\begin{smallmatrix}u\\ v\end{smallmatrix}\big)(x,d_{1}^{-1}t)\mapsto\big(\begin{smallmatrix}u\\ v\end{smallmatrix}\big)(x,t), one can reduce (1) to

(2) {ut+ux​x​x+b1~​u​ux+b2~​u​vx+b3~​ux​v+b4~​v​vx=0vt+α​vx​x​x+b5~​u​ux+b6~​u​vx+b7~​ux​v+b8~​v​vx=0(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+\widetilde{b_{1}}uu_{x}+\widetilde{b_{2}}uv_{x}+\widetilde{b_{3}}u_{x}v+\widetilde{b_{4}}vv_{x}=0\\ v_{t}+\alpha v_{xxx}+\widetilde{b_{5}}uu_{x}+\widetilde{b_{6}}uv_{x}+\widetilde{b_{7}}u_{x}v+\widetilde{b_{8}}vv_{x}=0\\ (u,v)\big|_{t=0}=(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{cases}

where α=d2d1∈ℝ∖{0}\alpha=\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}, (x,t)∈𝕋λ×ℝ(x,t)\in\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R} or ℝ×ℝ\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}, with 𝕋λ=[0,2​π​λ)\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}=[0,2\pi\lambda) for some λ>0\lambda>0. Note that we do not consider the case α=0\alpha=0 (i.e. d2=0d_{2}=0) or α=±∞\alpha=\pm\infty (i.e. d1=0d_{1}=0), since (2) is not dispersive in those cases.

When α=1\alpha=1, the basic techniques developed for the LWP of KdV by Kenig-Ponce-Vega [16] can be applied to (2) as discussed below, thus yielding the LWP of (2) in H−12​(𝕋λ)×H−12​(𝕋λ)H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) and H−34+​(ℝ)×H−34+​(ℝ)H^{-\frac{3}{4}+}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{-\frac{3}{4}+}(\mathbb{R}). However, when α≠1\alpha\neq 1, we show that there is an interval I0I_{0} such that particular resonances occur for α∈I0∖{1}\alpha\in I_{0}\setminus\{1\} and that the regularities for the LWP in both periodic and non-periodic settings need to be much higher than those for α=1\alpha=1. In particular, we use the Diophantine conditions to quantify this regularity in the periodic setting.

As a model example, we consider the local well-posedness (LWP) problem of the following system:

(3) {ut+ux​x​x+v​vx=0vt+α​vx​x​x+(u​v)x=0(u,v)|t=0=(u0,v0),⁡(x,t)∈𝕋λ×ℝ​ or ​ℝ×ℝ,\begin{cases}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+vv_{x}=0\\ v_{t}+\alpha v_{xxx}+(uv)_{x}=0\\ (u,v)\big|_{t=0}=(u_{0},v_{0}),\end{cases}\ (x,t)\in\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R}\text{ or }\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R},

where 𝕋λ=[0,2​π​λ)\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}=[0,2\pi\lambda) with λ≥1\lambda\geq 1, 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, and uu and vv are real-valued functions. We consider the Cauchy problem (3) with (u0,v0)∈Hs​(𝕋λ)×Hs​(𝕋λ)(u_{0},v_{0})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) or Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}). While we state and prove our results only for 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1 for the physical reason mentioned below, we discuss the corresponding results for other values of α≠0\alpha\neq 0. In particular, we have I0I_{0} = (0,4](0,4] for (3). See Remark 4.6.

The system (3) has been proposed by Majda and Biello [20] as a reduced asymptotic model to study the nonlinear resonant interactions of long wavelength equatorial Rossby waves and barotropic Rossby waves with a significant mid-latitude projection, in the presence of suitable horizontally and vertically sheared zonal mean flows. We henceforth refer to (3) as the Majda-Biello System. In [20], the values of α\alpha are numerically determined and they are 0.8990.899, 0.9600.960, and 0.9800.980 for different equatorial Rossby waves. Of particular interest to us is the periodic case because of more challenging mathematical nature of the periodic problem as well as the physical relevance of the proposed model (the spatial period for the system before scaling is set as 40,00040,000 km in [20].)

First, we review the recent well-posedness results for the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation:

(4) {ut+ux​x​x+u​ux=0u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x)∈Hs​(𝕋)​ or ​Hs​(ℝ).\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}u_{t}+u_{xxx}+uu_{x}=0\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\in H^{s}{(\mathbb{T})}\text{ or }H^{s}{(\mathbb{R})}.\end{array}\right.

Bourgain [8] proved the LWP in L2​(𝕋)L^{2}(\mathbb{T}) and L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) via the contraction mapping principle. Kenig-Ponce-Vega [16] improved Bourgain’s result and established the LWP in H−12​(𝕋)H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}) and H−34+​(ℝ)H^{-\frac{3}{4}+}(\mathbb{R}). Colliander-Keel-Staffilani-Takaoka-Tao [11] proved the corresponding global well-posedness results via the II-method. More recently, Christ-Colliander-Tao [10] proved the LWP in H−34​(ℝ)H^{-\frac{3}{4}}(\mathbb{R}) via the modified Miura transform and the LWP of the modified KdV, and Kappeler-Topalov [15] proved the global well-posedness of the KdV in H−1​(𝕋)H^{-1}(\mathbb{T}), using the complete integrability of the equation. (See [11] and the references therein.)

In this paper, we use the contraction mapping principle to show the LWP of (3), following the basic arguments in [8], [16], [11]. Before discussing how the KdV theory immediately yields the LWP of (3) (and (2)) when α=1\alpha=1, we list some basic properties of the Majda-Biello system (3). Several conservation laws are known for the system:

E1=∫u​𝑑x,E2=∫v​𝑑x,E3=∫u2+v2​𝑑x,E4=12​∫ux2+α​vx2−u​v2​𝑑x,E_{1}=\int u\,dx,\quad E_{2}=\int v\,dx,\quad E_{3}=\int u^{2}+v^{2}dx,\quad E_{4}=\frac{1}{2}\int u_{x}^{2}+\alpha v_{x}^{2}-uv^{2}dx,

where E4E_{4} is the Hamiltonian of the system. No other conservation laws seem apparent; whether the Majda-Biello system (3) is completely integrable is unknown. Also, the system has scaling which is similar to that of KdV and the critical Sobolev index scs_{c} is −32-\frac{3}{2} just like KdV.

In [8], Bourgain introduced a new weighted space-time Sobolev space Xs,bX^{s,b} whose norm is given by

(5) ‖u‖Xs,b​(Z×ℝ)=‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ξ3⟩b​u^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ,τ2​(Z∗×ℝ),\|u\|_{X^{s,b}(Z\times\mathbb{R})}=\big\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\widehat{u}(\xi,\tau)\big\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}(Z^{\ast}\times\mathbb{R})},

where ⟨⋅⟩=1+|⋅|\langle\>\cdot\>\rangle=1+|\cdot|, and the spatial Fourier domain Z∗=ℝZ^{\ast}=\mathbb{R} if the spatial domain Z=ℝZ=\mathbb{R} and Z∗=ℤ/λZ^{\ast}=\mathbb{Z}/\lambda if Z=𝕋λZ=\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}. Kenig-Ponce-Vega [16] proved that the sharp bilinear estimate

(6) ‖∂x(u​v)‖Xs,b−1​(ℝ×ℝ)≲‖u‖Xs,b​‖v‖Xs,b\|\partial_{x}(uv)\|_{X^{s,b-1}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})}\lesssim\|u\|_{X^{s,b}}\|v\|_{X^{s,b}}

holds for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4} and b=12+b=\frac{1}{2}+. Let S(t)=e−t∂x3S(t)=e^{-t\partial_{x}^{3}} and η⁡(t)\eta(t) be a smooth cutoff function supported on [−2,2][-2,2] whose value is 1 on [−1,1][-1,1]. Then, along with the linear estimates [18]:

{‖η⁡(t)​S​(t)​u0‖Xs,b​(ℝ×ℝ)≲‖u0‖Hxs​(ℝ)‖η⁡(t)​∫0tS⁡(t−t′)​N​(u⁡(t′))​d​t′‖Xs,b​(ℝ×ℝ)≲‖N⁡(u)‖Xs,b−1,\begin{cases}\vphantom{\bigg|}\|\eta(t)S(t)u_{0}\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})}\lesssim\|u_{0}\|_{H^{s}_{x}(\mathbb{R})}\\ \Big\|\eta(t)\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})N\big(u(t^{\prime})\big)dt^{\prime}\Big\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})}\lesssim\left\|N(u)\right\|_{X^{s,b-1},}\end{cases}

the bilinear estimate (6) and scaling establish the LWP of KdV (4) in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}. Clearly, the same argument applies to the non-periodic Majda-Biello system (3) when α=1\alpha=1. Hence, when α=1\alpha=1, (3) is locally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}.

In the periodic case, we have a weaker linear estimate on the Duhamel term [8], [11]:

‖η⁡(t)​∫0tS⁡(t−t′)​N​(u⁡(t′))​d​t′‖Xs,12​(𝕋λ×ℝ)≲‖N⁡(u)‖Zs​(𝕋λ×ℝ),\left\|\eta(t)\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})N\big(u(t^{\prime})\big)dt^{\prime}\right\|_{X^{s,\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}\lesssim\left\|N(u)\right\|_{Z^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R}),}

where ‖u‖Zs​(𝕋λ×ℝ)=‖u‖Xs,−12​(𝕋λ×ℝ)+‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ξ3⟩−1​u^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ2​Lτ1​(ℤ/λ×ℝ).\|u\|_{Z^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}=\|u\|_{X^{s,-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}+\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{-1}\widehat{u}(\xi,\tau)\|_{L^{2}_{\xi}L^{1}_{\tau}(\mathbb{Z}/\lambda\times\mathbb{R})}. This is due to the fact that b=12b=\frac{1}{2}. Strictly speaking, we need to use ‖u‖Ys=‖u‖Xs,12+‖⟨ξ⟩s​u^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ2​Lτ1\|u\|_{Y^{s}}=\|u\|_{X^{s,\frac{1}{2}}}+\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\widehat{u}(\xi,\tau)\|_{L^{2}_{\xi}L^{1}_{\tau}}, instead of Xs,12X^{s,\frac{1}{2}} norm, in order to control the C⁡([−T,T],Hs​(𝕋λ))C([-T,T];H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})) norm of solutions. However, this modification does not cause a serious problem, and we use Xs,12X^{s,\frac{1}{2}} norm for simplicity in the current discussion. The crucial bilinear estimate for the LWP of KdV is then:

(7) ‖∂x(u​v)‖Zs​(𝕋λ×ℝ)≲λ0+​‖u‖Xs,12​‖v‖Xs,12.\|\partial_{x}(uv)\|_{Z^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}\lesssim\lambda^{0+}\|u\|_{X^{s,\frac{1}{2}}}\|v\|_{X^{s,\frac{1}{2}}.}

Assuming the mean 0 condition on uu and vv, it is shown in [16] and [11] that the bilinear estimate (7) holds for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} with b=12b=\frac{1}{2} and fails for any b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} if s<−12s<-\frac{1}{2}. A key ingredient is the algebraic identity

(8) ξ3−ξ13−ξ23=3​ξ​ξ1​ξ2,forξ=ξ1+ξ2.\xi^{3}-\xi_{1}^{3}-\xi_{2}^{3}=3\xi\xi_{1}\xi_{2},\qquad\rm{for}\qquad\xi=\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}.

When α=1\alpha=1, the same estimates can be applied to the periodic Majda-Biello system (3) with the mean 0 assumption. Hence, along with the conservation of the means E1E_{1} and E2E_{2}, it follows that, when α=1\alpha=1, (3) is locally well-posed in H−12​(𝕋λ)×H−12​(𝕋λ)H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for the mean 0 initial conditions. We address the LWP theory without the mean 0 assumption in the appendix.

Now, let’s turn to the case 0<α<10<\alpha<1. In this case, we have two linear semigroups S(t)=e−t∂x3S(t)=e^{-t\partial_{x}^{3}} and Sα(t)=e−αt∂x3S_{\alpha}(t)=e^{-\alpha t\partial_{x}^{3}} corresponding to the linear equations for uu and vv, respectively. Thus, the Fourier transform of the solutions to the linear equation for uu is supported on {τ=ξ3}\{\tau=\xi^{3}\} and that to the linear equation for vv is supported on {τ=αξ3}\{\tau=\alpha\xi^{3}\}. Since α≠1\alpha\neq 1, they are supported on distinct curves, and this causes nontrivial resonance interactions which are not present when α=1\alpha=1. It turns out that the Cauchy problem (3) is locally well-posed in Hs​(𝕋λ)×Hs​(𝕋λ)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for s≥s∗=s∗​(α)s\geq s^{\ast}=s^{\ast}(\alpha), where s∗​(α)s^{\ast}(\alpha) ranges over (1/2,1](1/2,1] depending on the value of the coupling parameter α\alpha. In order to precisely quantify s∗s^{\ast} in terms of α\alpha, we need to go through some preliminaries.

For α≠1\alpha\neq 1, we need to define two distinct Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces. For s,b∈ℝs,b\in\mathbb{R}, let Xs,b​(𝕋λ×ℝ)X^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R}) and Xαs,b​(𝕋λ×ℝ)X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}\times\mathbb{R}) be the completion of the Schwartz class 𝒮⁡(𝕋×ℝ)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}) with respect to the norms

(9) ‖u‖Xs,b​(𝕋λ×ℝ)\displaystyle\|u\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{T_{\lambda}}\times\mathbb{R})} =‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−ξ3⟩b​u^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ,τ2​(ℤ/λ×ℝ)\displaystyle=\big\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\widehat{u}(\xi,\tau)\big\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}(\mathbb{Z/\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}
(10) ‖v‖Xαs,b​(𝕋λ×ℝ)\displaystyle\|v\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{T_{\lambda}}\times\mathbb{R})} =‖⟨ξ⟩s​⟨τ−α​ξ3⟩b​v^​(ξ,τ)‖Lξ,τ2​(ℤ/λ×ℝ).\displaystyle=\big\|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\tau-\alpha\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\widehat{v}(\xi,\tau)\big\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}(\mathbb{Z/\lambda}\times\mathbb{R})}.

The study of the periodic Majda-Biello system (3) will be based on the iteration in the spaces Xs,12×Xαs,12X^{s,\frac{1}{2}}\times X_{\alpha}^{s,\frac{1}{2}}.

For the following argument, assume λ=1\lambda=1 for simplicity. (For general λ≥1\lambda\geq 1, the implicit constants in (11) and (12) below depend on λ\lambda. See Propositions 3.7 and 3.8.) From the standard estimates on the Duhamel terms, the LWP of (3) follows once we establish the following bilinear estimates:

(11) ‖∂x(v1​v2)‖Xs,b−1​(𝕋×ℝ)\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(v_{1}v_{2})\|_{X^{s,b-1}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})} ≲‖v1‖Xαs,b​(𝕋×ℝ)​‖v2‖Xαs,b​(𝕋×ℝ)\displaystyle\lesssim\|v_{1}\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})}\|v_{2}\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})}
(12) ‖∂x(u​v)‖Xαs,b−1​(𝕋×ℝ)\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(uv)\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b-1}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})} ≲‖u‖Xs,b​(𝕋×ℝ)​‖v‖Xαs,b​(𝕋×ℝ).\displaystyle\lesssim\|u\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R})}\|v\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{R}).}

First, consider the first bilinear estimate (11). As in the KdV case [8], [16], [11], we define the bilinear operator ℬs,b​(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{B}_{s,b}(\cdot,\cdot) by

ℬs,b​(f,g)​(ξ,τ)=ξ​⟨ξ⟩s⟨τ−ξ3⟩1−b​12​π​∑ξ1+ξ2=ξ∫τ1+τ2=τf⁡(ξ1,τ1)​g​(ξ2,τ2)⟨ξ1⟩s​⟨ξ2⟩s​⟨τ1−α​ξ13⟩b​⟨τ2−α​ξ23⟩b​d​τ1.\mathcal{B}_{s,b}(f,g)(\xi,\tau)=\frac{\xi\langle\xi\rangle^{s}}{\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{1-b}}\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}=\xi}\intt_{\tau_{1}+\tau_{2}=\tau}\frac{f(\xi_{1},\tau_{1})g(\xi_{2},\tau_{2})}{\langle\xi_{1}\rangle^{s}\langle\xi_{2}\rangle^{s}\langle\tau_{1}-\alpha\xi_{1}^{3}\rangle^{b}\langle\tau_{2}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3}\rangle^{b}}d\tau_{1}.

Then, (11) holds if and only if

(13) ‖ℬs,b​(f,g)‖Lξ,τ2≲‖f‖Lξ,τ2​‖g‖Lξ,τ2.\left\|\mathcal{B}_{s,b}(f,g)\right\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}}\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}}\|g\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}}.

As in the KdV case, ∂x\partial_{x} appears on the left hand side of (11) and thus we need to make up for this loss of derivative from ⟨τ−ξ3⟩1−b​⟨τ1−α​ξ13⟩b​⟨τ2−α​ξ23⟩b\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{1-b}\langle\tau_{1}-\alpha\xi_{1}^{3}\rangle^{b}\langle\tau_{2}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3}\rangle^{b} in the denominator. However, when α≠1\alpha\neq 1, we no longer have such an identity and we have

we have (ξ1,ξ2)=(c1​ξ,c2​ξ)(\xi_{1},\xi_{2})=(c_{1}\xi,c_{2}\xi) or (c2​ξ,c1​ξ)(c_{2}\xi,c_{1}\xi), where

(16) c1=12+−3+12​α−16​ and ​c2=12−−3+12​α−16.c_{1}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{\sqrt{-3+12\alpha^{-1}}}{6}\ \text{ and }\ c_{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{\sqrt{-3+12\alpha^{-1}}}{6}.

Note that c1,c2∈ℝc_{1},c_{2}\in\mathbb{R} (with c1+c2=1\ c_{1}+c_{2}=1) if and only if 0<α≤4.0<\alpha\leq 4.

If c1∈ℚc_{1}\in\mathbb{Q} (and thus c2∈ℚc_{2}\in\mathbb{Q}), then there are infinitely many values of ξ∈ℤ\xi\in\mathbb{Z} such that c1​ξ,c2​ξ∈ℤc_{1}\xi,\>c_{2}\xi\in\mathbb{Z}. However, generally speaking, ξ−α​ξ13−α​ξ23\xi-\alpha\xi_{1}^{3}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3} can be arbitrarily close to 0, since c1​ξc_{1}\xi can be arbitrarily close to an integer. Therefore, we need to measure how “close” c1c_{1} is to rational numbers. We’ll use the following definition regarding the Diophantine conditions commonly used in dynamical systems.

Definition 1 (Arnold [2]).

A real number ρ\rho is called of type (K,ν)(K,\nu) (or simply of type ν{\nu}) if there exist positive KK and ν\nu such that for all pairs of integers (m,n)(m,n), we have

(17) |ρ−mn|≥K|n|2+ν.\left|\rho-\frac{m}{n}\right|\geq\frac{K}{|n|^{2+\nu}}.

Also, for our purpose, we define the minimal type index of a given real number ρ\rho.

Definition 2.

Given a real number ρ\rho, define the minimal type index νρ{\nu_{\rho}} of ρ{\rho} by

νρ={∞​, if ​ρ∈ℚinf{ν>0:ρ​ is of type ​ν}​, if ​ρ∉ℚ\nu_{\rho}=\begin{cases}\infty\text{, if }\rho\in\mathbb{Q}\\ \inf\{\nu>0:\rho\text{ is of type }\nu\}\text{, if }\rho\notin\mathbb{Q}\end{cases}
Remark 1.1.

Then, by Dirichlet Theorem [2, p.112] and [2, p.116, lemma 3], it follows that νρ≥0\nu_{\rho}\geq 0 for any ρ∈ℝ\rho\in\mathbb{R} and νρ=0\nu_{\rho}=0 for almost every ρ∈ℝ\rho\in\mathbb{R}.

Using the minimal type index of c1c_{1}, we prove, in Propositions 3.7 and 3.9, the bilinear estimate (11) holds for s≥min⁡(1,12+12​νc1+)s\geq\min(1,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}}+) with b=12b=\frac{1}{2}, and fails for b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} if s<min⁡(1,12+12​νc1)s<\min(1,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}}).

Let us now turn to the second bilinear estimate (12). In this case, the resonance equation is given by

(19) d1=−3​α+3​α​(4−α)2​(1−α)​ and ​d2=−3​α−3​α​(4−α)2​(1−α).d_{1}=\tfrac{-3\alpha+\sqrt{3\alpha(4-\alpha)}}{2(1-\alpha)}\ \text{ and }\ d_{2}=\tfrac{-3\alpha-\sqrt{3\alpha(4-\alpha)}}{2(1-\alpha)}.

Using the minimal type indices νd1\nu_{d_{1}} and νd2\nu_{d_{2}}, we prove, in Propositions 3.8 and 3.10, the bilinear estimate (12) holds for s≥min⁡(1,12+12​max⁡(νd1,νd2)+)s\geq\min(1,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\max(\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}})+) with b=12b=\frac{1}{2} under the mean 0 assumption on uu, and fails for any b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} if s<min⁡(1,12+12​max⁡(νd1,νd2))s<\min(1,\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\max(\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}})). Note that we need to take the maximum of νd1\nu_{d_{1}} and νd2\nu_{d_{2}} since we have d1+d2∉ℚd_{1}+d_{2}\notin\mathbb{Q} in general, unlike c1+c2=1c_{1}+c_{2}=1.

Finally, we state the main local well-posedness result. Let s0=12+12​max⁡(νc1,νd1,νd2)s_{0}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\max(\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}}). Note that s0=12s_{0}=\frac{1}{2} for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) in view of Remarks 1.1 and 3.12.

Theorem 1.

Let 0<α<10<\alpha<1 and λ≥1\lambda\geq 1. Assume the mean 0 condition on u0u_{0}. Then, the Majda-Biello system (3) is locally well-posed in Hs​(𝕋λ)×Hs​(𝕋λ)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for s≥s∗​(α):=min⁡(1,s0+).s\geq s^{\ast}(\alpha):=\min(1,s_{0}+). In particular, for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), the Majda-Biello system is locally well-posed in Hs​(𝕋λ)×Hs​(𝕋λ)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for s>12s>\frac{1}{2}. Moreover, the (real-valued) Majda-Biello system is globally well-posed in H1​(𝕋λ)×H1​(𝕋λ)H^{1}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{1}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) due to the conservation of the Hamiltonian.

This result is sharp in the following sense. Consider the solution map Φt:(u0,v0)∈Hs×Hs⟼(u⁡(t),v⁡(t))∈Hs×Hs\Phi_{t}:(u_{0},v_{0})\in H^{s}\times H^{s}\longmapsto\big(u(t),v(t)\big)\in H^{s}\times H^{s} for |t|≪1|t|\ll 1. Then, we have the following necessary conditions on the Sobolev index ss (This kind of result is often referred to as ill-posedness results. c.f. [17], [26].)

Theorem 2.

(a) If max⁡(νc1,νd1,νd2)>1\max(\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}})>1 and the solution map is C2C^{2}, then s≥1.s\geq 1. In particular, this result applies to the case when any of c1,d1,c_{1},d_{1}, or d2d_{2} is a rational number.

(b) If max⁡(νc1,νd1,νd2)≤1\max(\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}})\leq 1 and the solution map is C3C^{3}, then s≥s0s\geq s_{0}.

Therefore, if we require that the solution map is smooth (at least C3C^{3}), then the LWP theory on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda} is complete (except for the endpoint case s=12+12​max⁡(νc1,νd1,νd2)s=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\max(\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}}) when max⁡(νc1,νd1,νd2)<1\max(\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}},\nu_{d_{2}})<1 which leads to a number-theoretic question. See Remark 4.4.)

We’d like to point out the following. On the one hand the regularity index s∗​(α)s^{\ast}(\alpha) for the local well-posedness is 12+\frac{1}{2}+ for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). On the other hand, for any interval I⊂(0,1)I\subset(0,1), there exists α∈I\alpha\in I such that s∗​(α)=1s^{\ast}(\alpha)=1. This shows that the well-posedness (below H1H^{1}) of the periodic Majda-Biello system (3) is very unstable under a slightest perturbation of the parameter α\alpha. Also, note that α=1\alpha=1 is a special value since (3) is LWP for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} when α=1\alpha=1.

Lastly, note that we have stated Theorem 1 on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda} for λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 since in proving the global well-posedness on 𝕋\mathbb{T} (i.e. λ=1\lambda=1) via the I-method, we need to have LWP for λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 due to the scaling argument. See [22]. However, Theorem 1 itself holds on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda} for any λ>0\lambda>0 as long as λ\lambda is fixed.

Now, let’s discuss the LWP in the non-periodic setting for 0<α<10<\alpha<1. In this case, the LWP of (3) follows once we prove the bilinear estimates:

(20) ‖∂x(v1​v2)‖Xs,b−1​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(v_{1}v_{2})\|_{X^{s,b-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})} ≲‖v1‖Xαs,b​(ℝ2)​‖v2‖Xαs,b​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\lesssim\|v_{1}\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|v_{2}\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}
(21) ‖∂x(u​v)‖Xαs,b−1​(ℝ2)\displaystyle\|\partial_{x}(uv)\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b-1}(\mathbb{R}^{2})} ≲‖u‖Xs,b​(ℝ2)​‖v‖Xαs,b​(ℝ2).\displaystyle\lesssim\|u\|_{X^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}\|v\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}.

As in the periodic case, we obtain two resonance equations ξ3−α​ξ13−α​ξ23=0\xi^{3}-\alpha\xi_{1}^{3}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3}=0 and α​ξ3−ξ13−α​ξ23=0\alpha\xi^{3}-\xi_{1}^{3}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3}=0 with ξ=ξ1+ξ2\xi=\xi_{1}+\xi_{2}, giving rise to c1c_{1}, d1d_{1}, and d2d_{2}. Since the spatial Fourier variable ξ\xi is not discrete in this case, the rational/irrational character of c1,d1,c_{1},d_{1}, and d2d_{2} is irrelevant. In Propositions 5.3 and 5.4, we prove the sharp bilinear estimates (20) and (21) for s≥0s\geq 0 with some b=12+b=\frac{1}{2}+. Thus, we obtain

Theorem 3.

Let 0<α<10<\alpha<1. The Majda-Biello system (3) is locally well-posed in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥0s\geq 0. Moreover, the (real-valued) Majda-Biello system is globally well-posed in L2​(ℝ)×L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\times L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) due to the L2L^{2}-conservation law.

Moreover, this result is sharp in the following sense:

Theorem 4.

If the solution map is C2C^{2}, then s≥0s\geq 0.

Therefore, if we require that the solution map is smooth (at least C2C^{2}), then the well-posedness theory on ℝ\mathbb{R} is complete. Note that although the rational/irrational character of c1,d1,c_{1},d_{1}, and d2d_{2} is irrelevant in this case, the result for α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) is much worse than that for α=1\alpha=1, where the threshold is s=−34s=-\frac{3}{4}.

Remark 1.2.

There are several known results for (1). In [7], Bona-Ponce-Saut-Tom proved the LWP (for the Gear-Grimshaw system) in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>34s>\frac{3}{4}. Then, via the Xs,bX^{s,b} space and the bilinear estimate (6) in the non-periodic setting, further LWP and partial GWP results were proven in Ash-Cohen-Wang [3], Feng [12], Linares-Panthee [19], Saut-Tzvetkov [25] (also for KP systems on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}), where the best LWP result is proven in Hs​(ℝ)×Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) for s>−34s>-\frac{3}{4}. We’d like to point out that in [3], [19], and [25], it was assumed that A=(a11a12a21a22)A=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}\\ a_{21}&a_{22}\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) can be reduced to the identity matrix (1001)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) by similarity transformations and scaling changes. However, in general, AA can only be reduced to (100α)\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 0&\alpha\end{smallmatrix}\bigr) even if we assume that AA is self-adjoint and non-singular. Thus their results do not apply to the general KdV system (1), contrary to their claim. This is due to the fact that separate space-time scalings are applied to uu and vv in their work, which causes rescaled functions u~\widetilde{u} and v~\widetilde{v} to be evaluated at different space-time points (x,t)(x,t). In this case, a simple application of the bilinear estimate (6) is clearly prohibited. As one can see from Theorems 3 and 4, one can in general expect LWP on ℝ\mathbb{R} only for s≥0s\geq 0 if α≠1\alpha\neq 1. Also, see Alvarez-Samaniego and Carvajal [1].

In the appendix, by introducing the vector-valued Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces, we sketch the proof of the following theorem:

Theorem 5.

Let α=1\alpha=1 and λ≥1\lambda\geq 1. The Majda-Biello system (3) is locally well-posed in Hs​(𝕋λ)×Hs​(𝕋λ)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda})\times H^{s}(\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}) for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} (without the mean 0 assumption on uu and vv.)

This work is a part of the author’s Ph.D. thesis [21] at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. In two forthcoming papers on this subject, we address the global well-posedness via the II-method [22], and the invariant measures (i.e. the Gibbs measure as a weighted Wiener measure for a.e. α∈(0,4)\alpha\in(0,4) in [23] and the white noise for α=1\alpha=1 in [24]) and the almost surely global well-posedness on the statistical ensembles in the periodic setting.

This paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we introduce some standard notations. In Section 3, we make the precise statements of the bilinear estimates (11) and (12) on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda} for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 along with the basic linear estimates. Then, we prove Theorem 1. In Section 4, we prove the sharp bilinear estimates from Section 3 along with the counterexamples below certain regularities. In Section 5, we prove Theorem 3 by proving the corresponding sharp bilinear estimates in the non-periodic setting. In Section 6, we prove the ill-posedness results, namely Theorems 2 and 4. In the appendix, we introduce the vector-valued Xs,bX^{s,b} spaces, and sketch the proof of Theorem 5. Please see [21] for the full details.

3. Local Well-Posedness on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}, 0<α<10<\alpha<1

In this section, we first introduce the spaces for the solutions and the Duhamel terms along with known linear estimates and embeddings. Then, we give the precise statements for the bilinear estimates whose proofs are presented in the next section. At the end of the section, we present the proof of Theorem 1.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ϕ\phi be a periodic function on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda}. Then, we have

(24) ‖η⁡(t)​S​(t)​ϕ‖Xs,b≲‖ϕ‖Hs​ and ​‖η⁡(t)​Sα​(t)​ϕ‖Xαs,b≲‖ϕ‖Hs.\|\eta(t)S(t)\phi\|_{X^{s,b}}\lesssim\|\phi\|_{H^{s}}\text{ and }\ \|\eta(t)S_{\alpha}(t)\phi\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}}\lesssim\|\phi\|_{H^{s}}.

Remark 3.11.

The constant C⁡(λ)C(\lambda) of the bilinear estimate (7) for KdV is λ0+\lambda^{0+} and this does not cause any trouble in scaling for both local and global arguments (c.f. [11].) Unlike the KdV case, the LWP of (3) without smallness assumption of the initial data crucially depends on the fact that max⁡(C1​(λ),C2​(λ))\max(C_{1}(\lambda),C_{2}(\lambda)) can be controlled by λ32\lambda^{\frac{3}{2}}. Moreover, it is essential to minimize C1​(λ)C_{1}(\lambda) and C2​(λ)C_{2}(\lambda) for the application of the I-method for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 in establishing the global well-posedness of (3). See [22].

From Remark 1.1, we see that the minimal type index νc1=0\nu_{c_{1}}=0 for almost every c1∈ℝ.c_{1}\in\mathbb{R}. Similarly, we have νd1=νd2=0\nu_{d_{1}}=\nu_{d_{2}}=0 for almost every α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). The proofs of Propositions 3.8 and 3.10 for the second bilinear estimate (27) are analogous to those of Propositions 3.7 and 3.9, (using (35) and (36) instead of (33) and (34).) Note that |τ1−03|≤1|\tau_{1}-0^{3}|\leq 1 and |τ−α​N3|≤1|\tau-\alpha N^{3}|\leq 1 implies |τ2−α​N3|≤2.|\tau_{2}-\alpha N^{3}|\leq 2. Hence, if (51) holds, then, we must have N≲1N\lesssim 1 for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, which is impossible. Therefore, (30) (and hence (27)) can not hold for any s,b∈ℝs,b\in\mathbb{R}. ∎

We conclude this section by stating several important remarks.

Remark 4.3.

Unlike KdV (i.e. α=1\alpha=1), we do not need the mean 0 condition on the functions in Proposition 3.7. More importantly, while the resonance for α=1\alpha=1 makes the bilinear estimate (25) fail without the mean 0 condition regardless of regularity, the resonance for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 can be treated by assuming a higher regularity. This fact can be explained as follows. For example, the resonance for α=1\alpha=1 on 𝕋\mathbb{T} occurs when ξ1=ξ\xi_{1}=\xi and ξ2=0\xi_{2}=0 for all ξ∈ℤ\xi\in\mathbb{Z}. In some sense, we can say that there are infinitely many resonances accumulated at ξ2=0\xi_{2}=0. This makes it impossible to treat the resonance at ξ2=0\xi_{2}=0 and thus (25) for α=1\alpha=1 fails for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R} without the mean 0 condition.

Now, consider the case when 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Recall that, in dealing with (25), we have resonances at ξ1=c1​ξ\xi_{1}=c_{1}\xi and ξ2=c2​ξ\xi_{2}=c_{2}\xi for each ξ∈ℤ\xi\in\mathbb{Z}. Also, note that limα→1c1=1\lim_{\alpha\to 1}c_{1}=1 and limα→1c2=0\lim_{\alpha\to 1}c_{2}=0. Then, as soon as α≠1\alpha\neq 1, these infinitely many resonances accumulated at ξ2=0\xi_{2}=0 for α=1\alpha=1 are suddenly distributed over infinitely many distinct ξ2=c2​ξ\xi_{2}=c_{2}\xi for ξ∈ℤ\xi\in\mathbb{Z}, which lets us treat each resonance by assuming a higher regularity. This is what makes the α=1\alpha=1 case very different from α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1).

Remark 4.4.

When 0≤νc1<10\leq\nu_{c_{1}}<1, then the bilinear estimate (25) holds for s>12+12​νc1s>\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}} and fails for s<12+12​νc1s<\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}}. i.e. we are missing the endpoint s=12+12​νc1s=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}}. Actually, the proof of Proposition 3.7 can be applied to prove (25) for s=12+12​νc1s=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}} if c1c_{1} is of its own minimal type. i.e. if there exists K=K⁡(c1)>0K=K(c_{1})>0 such that for all pairs of integers (m,n)(m,n), we have

(52) |c1−mn|≥K|n|2+νc1.\left|c_{1}-\frac{m}{n}\right|\geq\frac{K}{|n|^{2+\nu_{c_{1}}}}.

Moreover, if (52) does not hold, then (25) fails for s=12+12​νc1s=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\nu_{c_{1}}. Showing (52) for given c1∈ℝc_{1}\in\mathbb{R} is a problem of number-theoretic nature, and we do not pursue this issue here. In Bambusi-Paleari [4] and Berti-Bolle [6], it is observed that the set A={c1∈ℝ:νc1=0A=\{c_{1}\in\mathbb{R}:\nu_{c_{1}}=0 and (52) holds}\} is uncountable and of measure 0. This implies that when νc1=0\nu_{c_{1}}=0, the bilinear estimate (25) holds for the endpoint s=12s=\frac{1}{2} only for c1c_{1} in this Cantor-like set AA of measure 0. The same remark applies to the bilinear estimate (27) in Proposition 3.8.

Remark 4.5.

In Proposition 3.8, we assume the mean 0 condition on uu. This is due to the infinite accumulation of resonance at ξ1=0\xi_{1}=0. (c.f. Remark 4.3.) If the mean of u0u_{0} is not 0, then we can consider (U,v)(U,v) instead of (u,v)(u,v), where U⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)−(2​π​λ)−1​u0^​(0)U(x,t)=u(x,t)-(2\pi\lambda)^{-1}\widehat{u_{0}}(0). Then, one needs to consider

(53) {Ut+Ux​x​x+v​vx=0vt+α​vx​x​x+(2​π​λ)−1​u0^​(0)​vx+(U​v)x=0.\begin{cases}U_{t}+U_{xxx}+vv_{x}=0\\ v_{t}+\alpha v_{xxx}+(2\pi\lambda)^{-1}\widehat{u_{0}}(0)v_{x}+(Uv)_{x}=0.\end{cases}

Note that this just adds a harmless first order linear term vxv_{x} in the second equation. See [8]. Also, note that the linear parts of (53) are not mixed unlike (68) in the appendix.

Remark 4.6.

c1,d1,c_{1},d_{1}, and d2d_{2} in defined (16) and (19) are real numbers if and only if α∈(0,1)∪(1,4]\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,4]. In particular, the same argument can be applied to establish the local well-posedness for α∈(0,1)∪(1,4]\alpha\in(0,1)\cup(1,4] whose regularity depends on νc1,νd1\nu_{c_{1}},\nu_{d_{1}}, and νd2\nu_{d_{2}}. When α=4\alpha=4, (3) is LWP on 𝕋λ\mathbb{T}_{\lambda} only for s≥1s\geq 1 since c1=12∈ℚc_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\in\mathbb{Q}. On ℝ\mathbb{R}, the proof of LWP seems to break down when α=4\alpha=4. See Remark 5.7.

When α<0\alpha<0 or α>4\alpha>4, the resonance equations (15) and (18) do not have a real solution for any ξ∈ℝ\xi\in\mathbb{R}. Let’s consider (25) in Proposition 3.7. From the resonance equation (15), we have

|ξ3−α​ξ13−α​ξ23|=|ξ|​|3​α​(ξ1−ξ2)2+(−1+α4)​ξ2|≳max⁡(|ξ1​ξ2​ξ|,|ξ|3).\displaystyle|\xi^{3}-\alpha\xi_{1}^{3}-\alpha\xi_{2}^{3}|=|\xi|\big|3\alpha\big(\xi_{1}-\tfrac{\xi}{2}\big)^{2}+(-1+\tfrac{\alpha}{4})\xi^{2}\big|\gtrsim\max(|\xi_{1}\xi_{2}\xi|,|\xi|^{3}).

Thus, we gain 32\tfrac{3}{2} derivatives and the bilinear estimate (25) holds for s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} (with the mean 0 condition) as in the KdV and α=1\alpha=1 case. The same remark applies to the second bilinear estimate (30) and the bilinear estimates (20) and (21) in the non-periodic setting. For example, see [1] for α=−1\alpha=-1 on ℝ\mathbb{R}.

5. Well-Posedness on ℝ\mathbb{R}, 0<α<10<\alpha<1

In this section, we establish the sharp well-posedness in L2​(ℝ)×L2​(ℝ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R})\times L^{2}(\mathbb{R}) for 0<α<10<\alpha<1 by proving the bilinear estimates (20) and (21). Let S(t)=e−t∂x3S(t)=e^{-t\partial_{x}^{3}} and Sα(t)=e−αt∂x3S_{\alpha}(t)=e^{-\alpha t\partial_{x}^{3}}. By standard computation [18], we have

Lemma 5.1.

Let ϕ\phi be a function on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Then, we have

(54) ‖η⁡(t)​S​(t)​ϕ‖Xs,b≲‖ϕ‖Hs​ and ​‖η⁡(t)​Sα​(t)​ϕ‖Xs,b≲‖ϕ‖Hs.\|\eta(t)S(t)\phi\|_{X^{s,b}}\lesssim\|\phi\|_{H^{s}}\text{ and }\|\eta(t)S_{\alpha}(t)\phi\|_{X^{s,b}}\lesssim\|\phi\|_{H^{s}}.
Lemma 5.2.

Let FF, GG be functions on ℝ×ℝ\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}. Then we have

‖η⁡(S∗RF)‖Xs,b≲‖F‖Xs,b−1​ and ​‖η⁡(Sα∗RG)‖Xαs,b≲‖G‖Xαs,b−1\|\eta(S*_{R}F)\|_{X^{s,b}}\lesssim\|F\|_{X^{s,b-1}}\text{ and }\|\eta(S_{\alpha}*_{R}G)\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b}}\lesssim\|G\|_{X_{\alpha}^{s,b-1}}

where ∗R*_{R} denotes the retarded convolution, i.e. S∗RF⁡(t)=∫0tS⁡(t−t′)​F​(t′)​d​t′S*_{R}F(t)=\int_{0}^{t}S(t-t^{\prime})F(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}.

Then, Theorem 3 follows once we prove (20) and (21). Indeed, the following propositions show that the estimates are sharp in Lx2​(ℝ)L_{x}^{2}(\mathbb{R}).

Proposition 5.3.

The bilinear estimates (20) and (21) hold for s≥0s\geq 0 with some b>12b>\frac{1}{2}.

Proposition 5.4.

If s<0s<0, the bilinear estimates (20) and (21) fail for any b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R}.

The proof of Proposition 5.3 is based on the usual argument with Hölder inequality, calculus lemmata, and change of variables in integration. (c.f. [16].) Since α≠1\alpha\neq 1, we need to separate the domain more carefully. First, we list some calculus lemmata.

For l>12l>\frac{1}{2}, we have

∫ℝd​x⟨x−α⟩2​l​⟨x−β⟩2​l≲1⟨α−β⟩2​l.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dx}{\langle x-\alpha\rangle^{2l}\langle x-\beta\rangle^{2l}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\langle\alpha-\beta\rangle^{2l}}.

∫ℝd​x⟨x⟩2​l​|α−x|≲1⟨α⟩12.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\frac{dx}{\langle x\rangle^{2l}\sqrt{|\alpha-x|}}\lesssim\frac{1}{\langle\alpha\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}}}.

6. On the Ill-posedness Results

There are also -so called- “ill-posedness” results for dispersive equations such as the KdV equation (4). However, this term often refers to the necessary conditions for uniform continuity or smoothness of the solution map Φt:u0∈Hs⟼u⁡(t)∈Hs\Phi_{t}:u_{0}\in H^{s}\longmapsto u(t)\in H^{s}. The Cauchy problem is not necessarily ill-posed in the sense of the usual definition, even when these results hold. However, since the contraction argument provides smoothness of the solution map it is often natural to consider a strengthened notion of well-posedness requiring the solution map to be uniformly continuous/smooth. In this latter sense, the following results may be regarded as “ill-posedness” results.

For KdV, Bourgain [9] proved that if the solution map is C3C^{3}, then s≥−34s\geq-\frac{3}{4} on ℝ\mathbb{R} and s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Tzvetkov [26] improved Bourgain’s result and showed that C2C^{2} is enough on ℝ\mathbb{R}. It was also shown that if the solution map is uniformly continuous, then s≥−34s\geq-\frac{3}{4} on ℝ\mathbb{R} and s≥−12s\geq-\frac{1}{2} on 𝕋\mathbb{T}. These results are obtained from the corresponding ill-posedness results of mKdV and the (modified) Miura transform, which is not available for the Majda-Biello system (3). See Kenig-Ponce-Vega [17] and Christ-Colliander-Tao [10].

When α=1\alpha=1, by setting v0=2​u0v_{0}=\sqrt{2}u_{0} and v⁡(t)=2​u​(t)v(t)=\sqrt{2}u(t), we see that (3) reduces to a single KdV equation: ut+ux​x​x+2​u​ux=0u_{t}+u_{xxx}+2uu_{x}=0. Hence, it follows from [10] that the solution map is not uniformly continuous for s<−34s<-\frac{3}{4} on ℝ\mathbb{R} and for s<−12s<-\frac{1}{2} on 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Let 0<α<10<\alpha<1. Following Bourgain [9], consider the following Cauchy problem:
